The wall thickness of the compressor, once the corrosion allowance has been added, is 35 mm, and this figure represents the thickness that is to be specified for fabrication. It is worth emphasising that the corrosion allowance forms an integral part of this figure, in the sense that the allowance has been included in order to ensure that the wall retains adequate thickness throughout the service life of the vessel as material is gradually lost to corrosion. The same allowance rule has been applied in the corresponding subsections that deal with the absorber and with the lean solvent pump, so a consistent basis is maintained across the section as a whole.

Attention now turns to the selection of the gasket material for the compressor joints, where a comparison has been carried out between the two candidate materials purely on the basis of temperature limit. Other properties that might in principle be relevant to the selection, such as chemical compatibility or mechanical behaviour, have not been compared at this stage, and the comparison should therefore be understood as resting on the temperature limit alone. On that basis, the material with the higher temperature rating is preferred, since it provides the greater margin between the rated limit and the conditions that the joint is expected to experience in service.

This preference, however, is not the end of the matter, because the margin that actually matters is measured against the temperature that the joint sees in service rather than against a nominal figure, and the service temperature at the joint is itself dependent on the operating state of the machine, which brings the discussion back to the conditions under which the compressor is required to run and the extent to which those conditions can be expected to vary.

The allowance is part of the specified thickness: the wall is sized so that the thickness remaining at the end of the service life, after the loss the allowance covers, still carries the design load. The absorber and the lean solvent pump are treated under the same allowance rule in their own subsections, and the basis is held across the section. A single rule applied to every vessel in the section keeps the fabrication specification consistent: no vessel carries an allowance another vessel lacks, and a reader comparing thicknesses across the section compares like with like.

The gasket selection for the compressor joints compares two materials on temperature limit only. No other property enters the comparison at this stage: chemical compatibility and mechanical behaviour are not assessed here, and the preference below rests on the temperature limit alone. On that basis the higher-rated material is preferred. Its rated limit stands further from the service temperature at the joint, and the margin between rating and service condition is the quantity the selection is intended to protect. A joint that runs close to the rated limit of its gasket has no reserve for the excursions that normal operation produces, and the preference for the higher rating is a preference for reserve at the joint, stated in the only terms the comparison supplies.
